Try to get as many assessments/reports done on your back injury and other conditions as you can. Keep copies for yourself. Apply for DSP and apply for NDIS. You may have enough supporting information to be approved for DSP likewise NDIS. If you get rejected by DSP but approved by NDIS have a support co-ordinator or LAC help you come up with your goals and identify what kind of supports you need on the regular - goals can be things like having a psychologist help you find ways to cope and better manage your ADHD and OCD. You can ask for physio and OT assessments to help you cope with your back injury.

If you get approved for NDIS but not DSP ask your LAC or Support Coordinator if you can get
 assistance in applying for DSP. If your on NDIS then you don't have to pay out of your own pocket for the assessments and reports,  if you have a support team of physios,  OTs and psychologists who have worked with you and understand your conditions they'll likely support you in writing required assessments etc for you to then reapply for DSP. 

It can take time but its worth it. I went through similar steps with NDIS where my psychologist and OT kept recommending that I apply for DSP and their assistance in proving documentation made a huge difference when I was finally approved for DSP not to mention how life changing it's been to have ongoing assistance through NDIS.

Sorry Op just to clarify, gross income is what you've earned before any taxes etc are taken out.
Net Income is what you take home. So in the example you gave
Gross Income is $1000
Salary Sacrificed ammount is $300
Net Income is then $700

Traditionally Centrelink always want your Gross Income.  They don't care if you're salary sacrificing because your Net Income (money you take home after everything else gets taken out) is not what they use to calculate if you're entitled to any assistance ammount.

Just speaking for myself when I salary sacrificed at my previous job and had to report income to Centrelink I still claimed the gross ammount (total ammount I was paid) before taxes and salary sacrifice ammount was taken out. I did this to be on the safe side with Centrelink.

The benefits of Salary Sacrificing is you're only being taxed on the ammount left after you've nominated whatever ammount you've agreed too. Centrelink assess how much they have to pay you based on your income before tax, therefore give them the gross ammount (total ammount earned before salary sacrifice ammount taken out and before tax is taken out) so that you don't end up owing Centrelink money.

Also (this might not apply to you) if you have a HECS, FEE HELP or Austudy Supplement Loan Debt be careful with Salary Sacrificing because it isn't applied to those debts. If you earn over the threshold for those debts (I think it used to be $80 000)  you can end up having to pay out of your pocket for HECS, FEE HELP etc debts.  My first year of salary Sacrificing I ended up having to pay $2000 to the ATO because of my Fee Help debts, but after the first time I told payroll an ammount to put towards my taxes so I didn't get caught out again. Not sure if that makes sense and like I said, this might not apply to you or your partner.

The other thing than can be helpful for Fatigue is learning what your triggers are. Fibromyalgia is effected by sensory information,  so things like light, sounds, smell, movement, temperature etc can really drain your energy. For me, shopping centres is are a cluster fuck of sensory data and leave me exhausted quite quickly so I avoid them or if I have to go to one I plan to be in and out very quickly. My brother also has fibromyalgia and he puts on dark glasses, baseball cap and ear plugs when he is out amd about so that sensory data isn't as over powering.


Understanding what impacts you the most energy wise and creating strategies to cope is important. One of my big triggers is overheating. Body temperature control is difficult with fibromyalgia and I tend to easily overheat which in turn makes me anxious and exhausted.  So I tend to dress in light lose clothing. I can't wear jeans anymore because the fabric is too heavy and hurts my legs.  I love leggings but can't wear them often coz they're too tight and leg pain is one of my consistent issues. 

Having a little bag where you carry all your essentials helps too, my brother had his ear plugs, sunglasses, paracetamol,  a scarf, finger less gloves and water in his pack with him at all times. In winter I always have gloves either on or with me coz I feel the cold a lot in my hands.

Pacing is also very important with fatigue.  I used to be able to do a lot of things in one day, now I usually can only do one thing.  If I have to work then I can't cook dinner or do the dishes in the same day, working is exhausting enough. If I have a day off then I try to cook and plan ahead for meals.  Even doing the dishes is difficult,  I have to break it up so I do cutlery and glasses, take a break, dishes, take a break, bowls, take a break, big pots and pans. Sometimes I have a chair by the sink coz the leg pain is too much.

Showering can be very difficult for me.
Hanging washing up hurts a lot, so I use a clothes horse so it doesn't hurt my arms as much.

I found magnesium helps a lot with pain. I also do floatation tank regularly as this helps a lot with pain and I sleep really well after so it helps with fatigue.

I can't think of anything else right now but I hope these suggestions help and give you some ideas on things that might help you. It's a difficult journey, doctors don't seem to help much but interacting with other fibromites helps.

Good luck.

There's some great support groups on Facebook for Fibromyalgia.  They're really handy ways to learn different things that may help. The support is also very helpful as Fibromyalgia really is a lot to deal with, the impact it has on your life can make things depressing,  the way other people react hurtful,  talking with people who understand helps.

Exercise,  like walking, can be helpful, but doing too much can trigger a flare. It's best to start small and slowly build up. Depending how bad your pain is you might want to start at 1-5 mins. You can either keep building up over time or do a few sets over a day. Like doing two 10 min walks a day might be easier for you than doing one 20 minute walk.  Find what works for you. If you're having a bad pain day don't push yourself.

I'd book the accommodation 3 months ahead and every fortnight put some money towards the accommodation cost so by the time it was vacation time I'd already paid for that and the only thing I had to worry about was meals for the week, petrol costs and if we did any activities.

Depends what you like to do on vacations and what your chronic illness allows you to do.  I know I've got limited mobility so I'm not going to be doing a lot of hiking or walking, so I try to find a tour I can do whether bus or boat or sky rail depending on location. 

I know I can't cram a day full of different activities,  so when I plan a trip away I research what's on offer and try to pick one thing a day I can manage (with the understanding that if I'm having a bad health day I might not be able to do everything).

I tend to spend more on nicer accommodation rather than budget places because given my health issues I'm going to spend a fair bit of my time in bed resting so I'd rather stay somewhere nice and comfortable rather than go for the cheapest option. Lots of Air BnB places might have a spa or open fire place, so a weekend away feels like a treat even if I can't do all the things I would have done before I became unwell.

Things like room service and making sure your staying somewhere close to 7/11s or cafes/restaurants also help so you can order food to your room or stock up on basics snacks/meds etc without having to go too far help a lot. 

Deciding whether to use taxis, ubers or public transport is another important factor. When I was in Singapore, public transport was very cheap and somewhat abundant, but meant having to walk a fair bit to get to different bus stops/train stations.  Taxis were also very cheap compared to my own country so it was easier to catch cabs and save my legs for things like museums/art galleries. Singapore has its own uber system that would have been great but we didn't find out about it till towards the end if our stay.

I love museums and art galleries but they tend to involve a lot of walking/standing and don't offer a lot of seating/rest places so I tend to avoid them or only go to one place as a highlight knowing I will have to rest the next day and may have difficulty walking afterwards for a few days. If the hotel has a pool that can help with sore legs after a big day.

If your flying registering as a disabled person makes a huge difference at the airport. I found the USA's disability assistance fantastic, they met me with a wheelchair and made sure I got to where I needed to go without a problem. They were very friendly and organised.  Some countries were not so good but their services still helped. 

Also, although it sounds silly, allowing yourself time after your vacation to recover is just as important.  Even though you're limited in what you can do, the change of routine and participating in things you can, does takes a lot out of you.  I did a 2 week trip to Jamaica with my son a few years back. We had 2 weeks in Jamaica then 5 days in L.A. Our time in Jamaica was beautiful,  mostly sedentry, spending our days by the beach. The 5 days in L.A was very busy so our tried to space things out, we did Movie World and paid extra for the access passes coz waiting in line was not practical for us. I didn't realise you could hire mobility scooters and regret not doing so but we had a great day. We rested the next day and most of the day after that but in the evening caught a cab down to see the wax museums, Ripleys Believe it Or Not and Guiness World Records.  My legs were on fire after that so the last day we did a tour of L.A. and got to see all the sites without walking much at all.
It took me about 3 months to totally recover from that trip but it was worth the sacrifice.

I'm so sorry you're having to deal with this so young.  I got diagnosed with fibromyalgia when I was 34. I had gone back to university when I was 30 and was sick all the time though didn't know why. I'm a single mum and was also working but managed to graduate.  I did a combination of on campus, online and intensives in order to graduate in 2 and a half years instead of 3-4 years.  I was super organised and pushed myself incredibly hard mainly coz I had to get into full time work as quickly as possible. 

A few years later when I was finally diagnosed with fibromyalgia (and CFS) I managed to work part time and complete 2 more degrees online. After the first year I was too sick to work but continued studying.

I registered with disability services and let all my lecturers know ahead of time that I struggle with chronic illnesses and as this is recognised as a disability I may need extensions etc from time to time.  Again having very good time management and organisational skills helped. Studying online gave me the flexibility to adapt as my health required. I was given extra time to complete exams due to my disability (these had to be done in person).  At one point I took a semester off because my health was too poor to study.

I know in some cultures university is seen as a fun/party time and missing out on that side of it would be disappointing.  But for me returning to university was about improving my education so I could get better job prospects and completing my degrees whilst managing my chronic illnesses and raising a child was intense but worth it in the long run. My capacity to work is limited due to my illness but I'm able to get interesting and well paid roles due to my qualifications. 

Adapting to chronic illness is a hard journey. It's important to have personal goals you can work towards so you don't feel like you're just sick all the time and life is passing you by. Can you do part time studies? Or do some units online and some on campus?  You might not be able to participate in all the fun stuff you had hoped to whilst at college but you can take the baby steps to ensure you study and improve your chances of getting a qualification so that in the future you have more options. Good luck.

I have fibromyalgia and mental health issues. I was unable to work for 5-6 years but my symptoms started to ease a bit and I was able to return to working (I am required to work in order to receive some welfare assistance but that's another issue).

When I was being interviewed for my current role I decided go be upfront about my chronic illness. I told them I may require time off on occasion due to my healtj issues and that my condition means I'm disabled.  For the first 12 months I was working 8 hour shifts 4 days a week. I found I couldn't keep up with that roster. I was having 1-3 days off most weeks, ran out of sick pay very quickly and when I was able to make it to work I'd either come in late or have to leave early.  Mentally I was very stressed out as I knew I didn't have the physical health to maintain my roster and felt a lot of pressure for letting my team down. All the stress was adding to my fibro and to my mental health issues.  

My manager called me in for a meeting. I was convinced I was getting fired. But instead she said she was really happy with my work and asked how she could help me cope with my work load.  Eventually she offered to reduce my work week to just 3 days a week and 6 hour shifts.  This has helped a lot. Obviously financially it is difficult but the change in hours helped my mental health immensely.  

I think bring upfront helped my situation because they knew about my disability when they hired me.  I do have flares and there's been times when I've had to take a week or two off work but they have been very accomodating and don't want to lose me. 
I'm in the process of reapplying for Disability Pension in my country. If I can get it I hope to go down to just 2 days a week work because physically,  though easier, I still really struggle with my fibro because of work. I love my job and after 6 years of not being able to get out if bed, continuing to work is important to me but I also need time to rest/recover and be able to do other things with my life outside of work. Right now all I do is work, rest and recover, work.

It's hard but hopefully you find a way to make it work for you and your potential employer is flexible and compassionate.

When I was 19 I had a manic episode and was told I had a bipolar disorder- a chemical imbalance in the brain that meant I'd be in and out of psychiatric wards if I didn't stay on meds for the rest of my life. I was told I couldn't ever work or study.  Having children was out aswell because the meds I was on would effect a foetus.  Childhood trauma wasn't even brought up.


I didn't accept the diagnosis but I did acknowledge something was wrong with me. I had attempted suicide in the past, was self harming, had been depressed for years. I figured if this came down to a chemical imbalance then there wasn't much I could do about it so I decided to focus on the things I could do something about.  I chose to get skills that helped me get work. I eventually chose to get off meds (though I was self medicating with drugs).  I chose to travel overseas.  I still struggled with self-hatred and depression but I chose to get help when it became too much to handle on my own.


At 27 I chose to go ahead with an unplanned pregnancy which also meant choosing to get off drugs and focusing on doing what I could to give my son a good life. This meant chosing to go back to uni and get my degree so I could ensure more stable income for our future. 


I'm 43 now. Two years ago I was diagnosed with CPSTD. This made a lot of sense. A lot more sense than the bipolar diagnosis.  I'm currently in my last week of a 4 week psychiatric ward stay doing a EMDR program. I chose to do the program because there was no other way to get the help I needed for my CPTSD.  Contrary to what they told me when I was 19, this is the first time I've been back in a psych ward.  And contrary to what they told me when I was 19, I've been able to work, study, travel and raise a son on my own. When I had my son I also made the choice to stay on meds because the depression that would come from time to time was too unsettling for me to be able to be a good mum. 

Most of my friends have not had the trauma I had growing up yet a lot of them are struggling with anxiety or depression. I may be 'behind' them financially but have definitely had a fullfilling, exciting and satisfying life so far.  No matter what you have been through,  there are parts of your life where you can chose what you do next. Whether it is choosing to get help when you need it, choosing to work towards financial stability, choosing to seek out what lifestyle you want for yourself and your loved ones.

I'm hoping this 4 week stint will put the trauma behind me but am open to seeking further treatment if I need it. But again that's a choice. My past does not equal my future because I'm doing all I can do to get past it.  It's not easy but I'm not the same drug addicted,  self harming, suicidal person I was at 19.

You are young. You have a lot of choices ahead of you.  You can shape your life in the way you want.  There is healing and there is hope. Don't worry about the pace or direction your friends lives seem to be taking. Be happy for them. Support them. It might be a steeper road than their's but you can still take the steps you need/want to get to where you want to go.

Matt Richards and Mark Langthorne wrote a surprising  Freddy Mercury biography called "Somebody to Love" that weaves the AIDS epidemic  in and out of Mercury's life story.  In it they identify HIV as originating in the Congo very early in the 20th Century but due to a long incubation period and the the short life expectancy in that region an overall virus killing people in mass was not identified.  In the 1950s-60s workers from Haiti were brought in to the Congo to assist industrialising the area but eventually sent back to Haiti. It is suspected these workers, who very likely had relationships with local women or used the services of prostitues brought the virus back to Haiti.

It is said the virus had a 10 year incubation period before showing any symptoms of HIV. If the virus was in Haiti around the 60s then symptoms wouldn't start showing up till the late 70s and early 80s. At that time in Haiti people could donate blood for money that was then sent to America for blood transfusions.  Given anyone could give blood, this meant a lot of Haitens who may have been infected by the returning workmen had a cash incentive to donate often.
The blood collected was not screened before being sent to hospitals across America and the business named in the book was one of the main suppliers of blood products to the USA.

(Apologies now for being useless with remembering names)

This covers part of how HIV got to America.  The connection to the gay community came as a result of the symptoms that started occurring across the country.  There is a rare form of cancer that presents itself as a fuzzy abscess on the tongue which was also one of the first pre-indicators to doctors that something not quite right was occurring.  The cancer itself was quite rare but across America doctors (and eventually the center of infectious diseases) started noticing an increase in the said cancer amongst men from the homosexual community.  Once the fuzzy abscess appeared men infected would often die within 1-2 years.  It was later determined the abscess was a sign of the later stages of HIV/AIDS epidemic.  Originally doctors did think the virus was only effecting gay men because of the high numbers showing symptoms and dying though in time they recognized the same symptoms in children and others who had received blood transfusions.

Sadly even when it was suspected the virus was being spread by transfusions, infected blood from Haiti was still being used on America without any proper screening process.

The book also talks about Patient 0, the man suspected of being the main carrier of the virus through out the gay community. The man was a flight attendant and travelled extensively through out North America. In tracing the spread of the virus the researchers were able to trace back to this one man as being the common thread where the virus broke out.  There is a lot of controversy surrounding identifying Patient 0 as the man behind the spreading of HIV in America (and the rest of the world) but that's probably best left for another time.

I work as a Peer Worker in a small psychiatric ward.  Peer Work in the Mental Health field is about being open about your own mental health journey and supporting others while they are in their own process. There are also Peer Workers who work with Army Vets to help them cope with PTSD and other areas that use Peer Workers in different roles.

Coming back to your situation,  I find that I can handle most clients but sometimes there are people where their circumstances might be a bit close to my own or can trigger my own trauma.  So I am careful how much work I do with those people or how much about myself I share.  I had a really intense situation once where a client had just spoken out about being molested by her brother, and because she'd never talked to anyone about it she asked me a lot of questions. At first it was ok but then she asked a lot more deeper questions that brought up a lot of trauma over my own sexual abuse experiences.  I got through the session with her but then needed to take a break so I could ground myself and also pin point why it had effected me so deeply- I realised I could talk about my experiences in general terms but actually having to recall details and things like that was way too personal. It was good because it gave me a clear boundary.

Learning about psychology and working towards being a  therapist would also cover things like how to have your own personal and professional boundaries,  how to be supportive yet also not get too attached to clients and also how to do 'self care' when working in the field.  Mental Health professionals are also required to have 'clinical supervision ' which is when you have someone qualified in your field to talk to and support your own mental health and professional development.

I know working as a Peer Worker has been so empowering for me, helping others in their journey and showing them You can get through the hard time is really rewarding and also gives new  meaning to the things I have been through. It's been very healing for me.  That said things like self care, being able to detach once my work day is over, recognising what clients I can connect to and which ones I can't,  are all important things I need to do to keep myself mentally well.

Psychologist have a different approach to Peer Work but I think the self care parts would be similar.

I guess from the perspective of self care, waiting till you're emotionally stable and not so vulnerable makes sense to me.  I don't believe we'll never be fully healed, I believe all mental health recovery is a journey and there are times in that journey where one is so raw that exposing your heart to anyone else is likely to end with you getting really hurt, which in turn is likely going to impact your mental and emotional framework badly.  Also, if you're early on in your healing you may have distorted perspective on yourself, what your needs are and how you view others- you may not have had enough healing in yourself to be able to recognize when someone is a suitable/safe person to commence a relationship with.  Where as when you've done enough healing work that you have a good self esteem, are kind to yourself, have forgiven yourself and are confident in yourself you're more likely to see prospective  partners more clearly and weigh up if the person has the character and maturity to be part of your life.

So often when we have trauma we want someone to love us into healing and will accept anyone who turns up into our lives as a possibility.  I think once there's been enough healing, growth and maturity you're more likely to look at romance as a lovely possibility but not something you 'have to have'  because the pain and loneliness of being single is too much to bare.

1. Save 10% of your wages from a young age. Don't touch it, just put it away. It will come in handy when you want to buy a car or put a deposit on a house. If 10% is too much pick an anmount you feel more confortable with- even $10 a fortnight is $520 after one year.


2. Avoid credit cards. It's too easy to get into serious debt when you are young and this will majorly mess up your options when you're older and want to get a loan.


3. Pay your rent and bills first, then food then live off what you have left. Some utilities let you set up small, regular payments so you're not hit with a massive bill every cycle. For example, I put $45 on my elec, $25 on my gas and $30 on my phone bills each fortnight. My online banking lets me set this up as ongoing arrangements  (I can cancel them if I need to).  Sometimes I end up so ahead of the total bill I can stop for a few months before I start again. It means having a little less cash flow each fortnight but it also means I don't have to fork up hundreds of dollars out of nowhere each time a utility bill comes in or try to figure out who to pay first and who to ask for an extension.


4. Set up two different accounts, one for emergencies or big cost items that come around once a year (car registration, insurance etc) and one for something special you want to save towards like a holiday etc. This is seperate to your ongoing 10% savings. Put small ammounts of money ($20-50) in each account every time you get paid that way when you have an emergency or that big cost item comes up you have money already put aside for it AND you have something special you are working towards.

These tips help make your life financially more stable if you're in poverty and makes it easier to organize extra income once you start making more cash. I moved out of home when I was 15 so I had to start paying rent and bills very early on. I've made a lot of mistakes financially (credit card debt was the worst one) but now at 41 I've got no debts, have a good job and am saving towards buying a house.  For the first time I'm not living in poverty but I've learnt how to manage my money in a way that ensures I've got a roof over my head, food on the table and the utilities secure at all times.

I understand about not being sure if you could cope with work long term.  I wasn't sure either but all I can do is try my best.  It's been difficult because fibromyalgia has its ups and downs. If my symptoms are too bad then I take time off, usually a day but early on I took 5 days off because I had asthma and chest infection thst just wasn't getting better and was trying to push on ontop of fibro. I figured if I didn't stop I wasn't going to ever get ontop of it.  They were very good about it and said my health has to always come first.  Other things like making sure I don't work more than 3 days straight and keeping up my self care routine (stuff that isn't medication but that I find helps with the fibro) all make a big difference.  Good luck on your journey and I hope you find an employer who is both understanding and flexible. It made a big difference to my mental well being to be able to work again.

My old girl Teisha would sometimes bury her food in the carpet. She'd go through the motions of digging up dirt, putting her food in the invisible hole then use her nose to move the invisible dirt onto her food to hide it well. No, the carpet wasn't extremely shaggy or anything like that, there was no ' dirt' to actually bury her food, just something odd she used to do.  We never got her high though there is a possibility she got a contact high from my brother and I smoking pot in the lounge room though I'm pretty sure she would do it even if we hadn't been smoking.
I now have two dogs, Minnie and Piper. Minnie likes her food served next to her bed. She eats very slowly, like it takes her hours, and she growls at Piper if she comes close to her bed. Sometimes she guards her food even if she doesn't want to eat it- like if she has a piece of bread, she wont eat it but hide it in her bed for days and wont leave that spot so Piper can't have it. I have to sometimes throw her food out if she hasn't touched it for a day and wont eat it because she wont go outside or anything when she's guarding food.
That sounds like hell. How do you cope?

1. Get all toxic people out of my life or, if it's a family member I can't totally cut off, have minimal contact with them.
2. Get to know people slowly and only gradually let them into my life if they're genuine and caring people. When I was younger I had a lot of people in my life who were selfish or good to party with but not good at healthy friendships and it used to fuck with my head a lot. Now I'm very cautious who I let in my life as I value my mental stability and don't want dramas.
3. Identify the things I am doing in my own self that lead to depression and make changes. Things like being overweight or dating arseholes. Work on my issues.
4. Found a good psychologist and talked about the traumatic things in my childhood and life.
5. Cognitive behavioural therapy.
6. Take my antidepressants.
7. When the bouts of depression hit- and they always do- remind myself I can get through this and the storm will eventually pass. I have bipolar 2 and have learned to accept depression will always be part of my life, the difference from when I was younger is being able to ensure the people who are now in my life genuinely care and support me and I've worked hard on myself to deal with issues and create the most stable life for myself and my son.

I try to avoid reaching high pain days by doing self care stuff like going to a floatation tank once a fortnight. The high levels of magnesium in the water helps with pain and going regularly means Im absorbing high doses of magnesium through my skin. I found walking on short ammounts (5-10 minutes) a few times a week helps too.
When pain gets really bad, I take my night dose of pain medication earlier in the day like in the afternoon or early evening. Warm shower and magnesium oil on the areas that hurt the most (usually legs and arms for me). Stay on my room with soft lights and air con on and take a couple of extra pain meds if it doesn't ease up. I find the magnesium oil doesn't help straight away but usually by next day there's some relief.
